title: Capstone RBAC Server — Startup & Audit Log
caption: A centralized RBAC and identity server built with a five-person capstone team: RS256-signed JWTs carrying roles and permissions, validated end-to-end from login through a downstream service.
alt: Terminal output from docker compose up: the Postgres database initializing its schema and seed data and reporting healthy, the auth engine warning that no private key file was found so it falls back to a temporary in-memory RS256 key, the Core Authentication Engine starting on port 8080, the downstream mock service delegating authorization checks to it, and audit log lines showing a login and a token validation both granted to the admin role.

title: AWS Cloud Resume — S3 Bucket
caption: The S3 bucket this site deploys to, showing the actual build output: 404 page, blog and resume folders, sitemaps, and the Astro built index.html, all served through CloudFront.
alt: AWS S3 console showing the carsonfarinella.com bucket's root objects: 404.html, blog/, favicon.ico, favicon.svg, gallery/, images/, index.html, resume/, scripts/, sitemap-0.xml, sitemap-index.xml, and workbench/ — the actual build output this site deploys from.

title: Before & After — Moving to Astro
caption: The first version was hand-written HTML and CSS with no build step — every page a copy-paste of the last. The rebuild moved it onto Astro components and content collections, with a GitHub Actions build that compiles the site and deploys the output to the same S3 and CloudFront.
alt: Side-by-side comparison of the site before and after the Astro rebuild. Left: the original resume, a single centered white card on a grey page, built from one hand-coded HTML file. Right: the current site, a wide editorial layout with a large Fraunces serif wordmark and a working-notes section, built from Astro components and deployed by a GitHub Actions pipeline.

title: BirdCage — First Traffic Observer Run
caption: BirdCage is an Android app I’m building, still in early development. This is its first on-device run: a local VpnService taps one app’s traffic for the length of a session and names the third-party companies it contacted, using TLS SNI and DNS matched against an offline tracker dataset. 13 of 35 flows (33 of 34 MB) came back opaque because they were QUIC, so the next step was decoding QUIC v1 Initial packets to recover their SNI as well.
alt: Dark-themed Android debug screen titled Domain observer, 3 sessions measured. A Reddit session from Sep 3 lists 2 distinct third-party companies, AppsFlyer and Google, across 14 hosts, with 13 of 35 flows opaque (33 MB of 34 MB), all of them QUIC. Below is a per-host table: each row shows a hostname or IP, its owning company, a category, how it was identified (SNI or none), and bytes transferred — led by an unidentified IP at 33 MB, then gql-fed.reddit.com at 586 kB, down to v.redd.it at 7.1 kB.
